newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-OPINION - Louthean on Australian Mining - Digging deeper.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-OPINION - Louthean on Australian Mining - Digging deeper.

text.p: By Ross Louthean*
A year ago the mine finding ability in Australia was a thorny issue - despite the dollars going into the ground there was a drought of almost two years.
However, even the discoveries since, while seen as promising, have not as yet shown themselves to be elephants.

There have been good finds by Sipa Resources International NL in northern Western Australia, by the new explorers in the WA sector of the Tanami Desert and the sniffs are getting stronger in the Gawler Craton of South Australia. But the real lift in Australian reserves of late has come from not picking up greenfield discoveries or step out drilling at existing mines but from digging deeper.

The September round of quarterly reports have been a shot in the arm for ailing spirits with at least three prime examples - Great Central Mines NL at Bronzewing and its new Jundee mine and the equally new neighbour, Eagle Mining Corporation NL's Nimary mine. Further south, near the once-despised salt lake country under Laverton, Acacia Resources Ltd showed it has an exciting deep target near its Sunrise Dam mine project. This development will also be a spur for the neighbouring Red October joint venture between Sons of Gwalia Ltd and Mt Burgess Gold Mining Co NL.

While it may take the share market some time to wake up to the importance of the progress by these companies, the important fact is that these new deep finds, while in some cases showing good signs up to six months ago, now have scope for good tonnes (of commercial ore) per vertical metre.

That's a term mining engineers dealing with an underground development like to hear, and directors and others taking the risk will be encouraged by the fact that good grades are also coupled with the tonnes per vertical metre.

The projection made about six months ago by Great Central Mines's resources director Eduard Eshuys that Jundee was showing signs of high grade mineralisation at depth was given resounding support by the September quarter report.

The Bartons Deep target which gave some excellent sniffs in the June quarter report now has produced wide intersections of high grade mineralisation, prompting Great Central (GCM) to retain five drill rigs to probe for extensions. It alters the picture of Jundee being a large shallow oxide target that last year started out with only five years mining life, and that was virtually lateral.

The search success at Jundee was matched by more high grade mineralisation below the Discovery and Central pits at Bronzewing -- and also had more significant drill intersections at the Mount Joel prospect, north of Bronzewing.
Some observers, including GCM executive chairman Joseph Gutnick, believe Mt Joel could be the company's next mining cab off the rank in the Yandal belt.

Testing below 100 metres at the Barton deposit at Jundee has shown high grade mineralisation extends over a strike length of 800 metres and a known vertical depth of 250m and remains open to the north, south and a depth.
MULTIPLE LODES AT DEPTH IN THE BARTON DEPOSIT AT JUNDEE
Last drilling has shown multiple lodes similar to structures picked up in the top 100m profile and is presently being mined.

Better drill results from Bartons Deep were -- JRCD5384:: 13m from 306m depth grading 38.3 g/t; JRCD5671: 6.5m from 321.5m at 43.5g/t; JRCD5586: 4.1m from 295m at 59.9 g/t; JRCD1013: 8m from 258.5m at 28.6 g/t; JRCD1051 10.5m from 191m at 14.4 g/t; JRCD5700: 10m from 289m at 8.9 g/t; JRCD5828: 7.5m from 329m at 10.9 g/t.

At Bronzewing, the latest drilling below Discovery pit must help with the blueprint on developing the untapped ore positions. GCM now appears to have dispensed with the idea of extending the open cut, as an evaluation has shown ore pockets and any new extensions could be more economically accessed through underground method on the Discovery Deeps.
Best results was a hit of 10m at 52.g g/t under the Discovery pit and an equally spectacular hit near the massive Shoot 39 which is the dominant underground mining structure at Bronzewing.

Other results include 39m at 11.9 g/t, 13m at 22.1 g/t and 49m at 8.1 g/t near the Central mine's 6 level and 17m at 15.1 g/t and 28.1m at 28.3 g/t just below that mining block and, near lower levels, intercepts of 15m at 17.9 g/t, 55m at 8.7 g/t and 78.4m at 11 g/t.
Below the base of the nearby Discovery pit the ore enhancement included drill hits of 56m at 4.5 g/t, 10.9m at 52.6 g/t, 14.8m at 20.8 g/t and 15m at 42.9 g/t.
Clearly, these results fuel the imagination that Bronzewing has a lot of blue sky ahead in being one of the richest grade and biggest underground gold mines in Australia.

Certainly, its cash costs, taking in ongoing underground development costs of A$248/ounce are impressive for a period carrying high capital expenditure. So, is Jundee which came in with cash operating costs for the September quarter of A$245/oz.

In the quarter Bronzwing milled from the Discovery pit and from underground operations 386,206 tonnes at 6 g/t for 72,318 oz, at a mill recovery of 97.7 percent. Jundee milled 700,218t of open pit ore at 2.8 g/t for 60,068 oz, at a recovery of 96.7 percent.
At Mt Joel drilling picked up what may be a parallel structure east of the known ore system.
Better results included MJRB988: 48m from 12m at 7.4 g/t; GJRC465: 12m from 12m at 8 g/t; GJRC511: 15 from 97m at 9.5 g/t; GJRC500: 13m from 80m at 3.2 g/t; GJRC457: 16m from 36m at 2.7 g/t.

On the milling front, a feasibility is due soon on expanding the Jundee mill and the A$2 million upgrade of the Bronzewing plant -- to bring its capacity to two million tonnes per annum -- should be completed by the end of next February.
Gas conversion studies to utilise the new Goldfields Gas Pipeline are to be completed by the end of the current quarter.

Cash and bullion for GCM at the end of September was A$30.2 million and the company drew down a further A$25 million gold loan from Dresdner Australia Ltd for a repayment to prospector Mark Creasey, the original prospecting partner on Bronzewing, Jundee and many other GCM properties in the Yandal belt.
A healthy first operating year profit, healthy operating costs and reaching the milestone of production 100,000 ounces have been highlights for Eagle Mining Corporation.
BLUE SKY DOWN UNDER IN JUNDEE AND NIMARY DEEPS

The Nimary mine, which poured its first gold late last year about the same time as Jundee was commissioned, was behind a maiden net profit of A$7 million, after allowing A$7.9 million for deprecation and amortisation, and in the September quarter produced 31,697 ounces at a net cash cost of A$203/oz. In the third week of October the mine poured its 100,000th oz.
Intensive drilling of the western zone of the Nim3 deposit lifted the mine's proven and probable reserve by 122,700 oz to 734,200 recoverable oz.
Nim3's proven-probable reserve is now 2.673 million tonnes at 6 g/t. This zone's pit has now been optimised to a depth of 290m, representing an increase of 110m on the previous design.
Eagle has approved a budget of A$7 million to June next year to continue near-mine exploration with a prime focus on Nim1 and Nim3.
Better results (uncut) were:-NRC1697: 14m from 58m at 11.75 g/t; NRC1751: 6m from 70m at 94.49 gt; NRC1752: 13m from 168m at 13.16 g/t; NRC1778: 14m from 133m at 24.59 g/t.

Continuing work at Nim3's western zone included:- NRC1643: 5m from 154m at 25.86 g/t; NRC1678: 1m from 147m at 15.65 g/t and 3m from 68m at 14.39 g/t; NRC1679: 1m from 124m at 20.13 g/t and 9m from 146m at 21.36 g/t; NRC1702: 12m from 110m at 37 g/t (14.38 g/t cut to 80 g/t); NRC1712: 2m from 133m at 15.25 g/t and 8m from 145m at 79.24 g/t (28.64 g/t); NRC1717: 3m from 159 at 26.62 g/t and 11m from 166m at 154 g/t (28.28 g/t); NRC1771: 3m from 207m at 23.1 g/t; NRC1783: 9m from 151m at 12.16 g/t and 6m from 172m at 78.58 g/t (44.41 g/t); NRC1784: 4m from 173m at 17.63 g/t; MET1 (diamond hole): 7m from 43m at 36.34 g/t (19.2 g/t): NDH178: 7m from 128m at 29.39 g/t (26.88 g/t), 9.5m from 144m at 9.77 g/t, 8m from 193m at 2.96 g/t and 2m from 261m at 6.27 g/t.

Jundee and Nimary cover the same mineralised structure and there is one shared open cut operation and may be others as mining progresses. Originally, it was said Nimary had the grade and Jundee the tonnes.
Based on the September quarter results, where the blue sky is definitely down under, it could be said that both in underground terms may have both the tonnes and grade.
* Ross Louthean is editor of Paydirt and publisher of Gold Mining Journal, The Australian Mines Handbook and Mineral Resources of New Zealand.
